These are the companions, or the social life, or the trinkets, or the diversions of people, and the kindness of others; they tear him here and there and pull at his heart and his inwardness, so that he must necessarily rot in all divine life and in divine seriousness, and he does not feel God’s grace and devotion. For a person, this small temptation is often much more harmful than the great afflictions, for the person guards himself against the latter with diligence and considers them to be wrong, but the person does not want to heed these small defects, nor consider them to be wrong. In the same way that all things one does not acknowledge are much more harmful than those one does acknowledge, so too is this danger, which one does not value or heed much, such as companionship, social life, or pleasure in creatures. Just as the deer is heated by every hunt, and its thirst increases all the more through it, so should a person be heated by every temptation for divine love toward our Lord, and be stimulated or driven by every affliction, in true thirst, to run more and more into God, where he finds nothing but truth, joy, righteousness, and comfort. <note>*)</note>

Now, sometimes hunters do this: when the deer is too tired and too thirsty, they feed the hounds a little, and in this way they are held back. When they are sure of the deer in the game park, they let the deer walk about a little so that it is somewhat strengthened by this, so that it may then better endure the hunting. Our Lord does the same for a person when He sees that the hunting is becoming too much for him, and the affliction too great; He holds them back a little, and then a drop falls into the mouth of the person’s heart, that is, a sweet taste of the sweetness of divine things, which strengthens him so much that all things that are not God taste bitter and adverse <note>original: "widerzehme"</note> to him, and then it seems to him that he has entirely and utterly overcome all his distress.

To summarize everything stated so far in one concept, it is necessary first to remind the reader that the discussion here is not about the origin of experience, but about what is contained within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology and, even there, could never be properly developed without the latter, which belongs to the critique of knowledge and especially of the understanding.

Experience consists of intuitions <note>original: "Anschauungen"</note>, which belong to sensibility, and of judgments, which are merely a task of the understanding. However, those judgments that the understanding makes merely from sensible intuitions are by no means yet judgments of experience. For in the former case, the judgment would only connect perceptions as they are given in sensible intuition, whereas in the latter case, the judgments must state what experience is in general, and consequently what it contains, rather than mere perception, the validity of which is merely subjective. Thus, a judgment of experience must add something more to the sensible intuition and the logical connection thereof (after they have been made universal through comparison) in a judgment, something that determines the synthetic judgment as necessary and thereby as universally valid. But to say that it is good, one must further direct it through reason toward purposes, namely, that it is a state that makes us fit for all our activities. Regarding happiness, everyone finally believes they can call the greatest sum (in terms of both quantity and duration) of the enjoyments of life a true, and indeed the highest, good. But reason struggles against this as well. Pleasantness is enjoyment. If, however, one aimed solely at this, it would be foolish to be scrupulous regarding the means that provide it, whether it were obtained passively, from the bounty of nature, or through self-activity and our own efforts. But that the existence of a human being who lives merely to enjoy (and is in this regard even very busy) should have an absolute value, even if he were of the best service to others who also only aim at enjoyment, and indeed because he shared in all their pleasure through sympathy, is something reason will never be persuaded to accept. Only through what he does, without regard to enjoyment, in full freedom and independently of what nature might provide him even passively, does he give his existence, as the existence of a person, an absolute value; and happiness, with the whole fullness of its pleasantness, is by no means an unconditional good.*)

### *On the proportionality of the limbs.* Chap. CLXXV.

ALL the parts of any animal must be correspondent to its whole, meaning that a creature which is short and thick must have every limb short and thick in itself, and one that is long and thin should have long and thin limbs, and a mediocre one should have limbs of the same mediocrity. I intend the same to be said for plants that have not been stunted by man or by winds, because these place youth over old age, and thus their natural proportionality is destroyed.

We asked them which way we should go, and that they inform us of the road, because they did not want to go there. They told us the road was up that river toward the North, and that for seventeen days we would find nothing else to eat but a fruit they call <term>chacan</term> <gloss>a type of desert fruit/root</gloss>, which they mash between stones; even after doing this, it can hardly be eaten, it is so bitter and dry. And indeed it was the truth, because they showed it to us there and we could not eat it. They also told us that while we traveled up the river, we would always be among people who were their enemies and spoke their same language, and that they would have nothing to give us to eat, but that they would receive us with very good will and would give us many cotton blankets, hides, and other things they possessed. However, they still felt that we should by no means take that road. Doubting what we should do, and which path would be more to our purpose and benefit, we delayed with them for two days.

They gave us beans and squashes to eat. The way they cook them is so novel that, because it is so, I wanted to put it here, so that it may be seen and known how diverse and strange are the inventions and industries of human beings. They do not have pots, and to cook what they wish, they fill a large gourd halfway with water and throw into the fire many stones that they can most easily heat. They take them while burning with wooden tongs and drop them into the water in the gourd until they make it boil with the heat the stones carry. When they see that the water is boiling, they throw into it whatever they are going to cook. All this time, they do nothing but take out some stones and throw in others that are burning so that the water stays boiling to cook what they want, and in this way they cook it.
